name: Manuka honey mask
lead: A manuka honey mask is mānuka honey spread over the face and left on before rinsing. People use it to calm breakouts, soften skin and give it a smoother, more hydrated look, and it is a staple of at-home skincare routines.

Mānuka honey is made from the nectar of Leptospermum scoparium, native to New Zealand and coastal Australia; its activity is attributed in part to methylglyoxal and graded by systems such as UMF and MGO. [1] A 2013 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes honey in skin care as an emollient, humectant and soothing ingredient found in cleansing milks, creams, lip products and masks, with antimicrobial activity attributed to hydrogen peroxide or, in manuka, methylglyoxal. [3]

Laboratory work indicates manuka honey shows antibacterial effects even when hydrogen peroxide activity is blocked, and medical-grade honeys have been tested against resistant bacteria in vitro. [4] Wound-care trials in humans exist for honey; trials specifically of a manuka honey face mask for acne have not been published.

paras: The 2013 dermatology review notes honey's use in cosmetic formulations at concentrations from about 1 to 10 percent, and up to 70 percent when mixed with oils, gels or emulsifiers. [3] It also records historical use of honey on skin across early civilizations and use in treatments for conditions such as seborrhea, dandruff and psoriasis. [3] A 2014 American Family Physician review of impetigo lists manuka honey among natural remedies reported as anecdotally successful, without enough evidence to recommend it. [5]

Mānuka honey is graded by methylglyoxal content (mg/kg) and by the trademarked UMF scale [1]. The UMF Honey Association says roughly six times more honey is sold internationally as mānuka than New Zealand produces, and UK tests in 2011-2013 found most mānuka-labelled samples lacked expected non-peroxide activity [1].

Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster burn healing, moderate evidence for post-operative wounds, and low-quality evidence for other wound types; several medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns [2]. Honey is not recommended for infants under one year because of botulism risk [2].

No studies found on manuka honey face masks for acne or skin appearance. Honey has been studied in wound and burn care, where Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster burn healing. [2] Randomized trials have tested manuka honey on eyelid wounds and in chronic rhinosinusitis irrigation. [6][7]

A 2011 review states that non-peroxide activity in manuka honey comes with low pH and high sugar content that hinder microbial growth, and that antimicrobial activity varies widely between honeys depending on nectar sources. [4] Trials of manuka honey in other settings, such as eyelid wound healing and nasal irrigation for sinusitis, have been published. [6][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, a thread titled around "honey maxxing" presents daily honey washing and masks as a route to better skin. [8]

claims.claim: Washing and masking with raw or manuka honey gives soft, high-quality skin, even with acne scars.
claims.believers: The original poster says nightly masks and honey washes leave skin soft and never dry, unlike other products. [8]
claims.experts: A dermatology review describes honey as a humectant and soothing cosmetic ingredient. [3] No trials of honey masks on acne scars have been published.

claims.claim: Scrubbing with honey exfoliates and grows new skin layers.
claims.believers: The poster recommends a raw honey scrub several times a week. [8]
claims.experts: Other forum members replied that honey is a good humectant but not a cure-all, and cautioned against scrubbing the face frequently. [8]

card.summary: Manuka honey smeared on the face for acne; wound studies exist for honey, but none for acne were found.
card.note: Authenticity and grading of manuka products are disputed.

quick.overview:
People apply manuka honey as a face mask to calm acne and skin.

Honey has some wound-care evidence, but no acne studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to methylglyoxal and antibacterial activity seen in lab studies; effects on acne are untested.
quick.risks: Honey is generally safe in food amounts; labelling and authenticity of manuka honey are disputed. Honey is advised against for babies.

chain: Honey applied as a face mask
Humectant and soothing effects plus antibacterial activity
Softer, hydrated skin and calmer-looking breakouts
angle.text: Users leave honey on the face as a mask or wash with it daily, saying it leaves skin soft, hydrated and less irritated, and some say it helps acne marks look better over time.
